title: The Armenian Catholics
hook: heirs of the first nation to adopt Christianity

segments.voice: Yesterday, Coptic and Ge'ez Catholics: Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea, and a man in a chariot reading Isaiah. Your line was africa's ancient churches. Whom did you stay to help? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

"The ark rested … upon the mountains of Armenia." That's Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, at the end of the flood. Noah's boat comes to rest, and the name on the map is Armenia. Armenians call a great snow-capped mountain on their horizon Ararat, and tradition ties it to that story. But the story at the center of Armenian Christianity comes much later, and it begins in a pit. A man thrown into a deep hole in the ground by a king, left there to die. Today, the church that came out of that pit, and the Catholics who belong to it.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS OF ARMENIA.` → `ARARAT ON THE HORIZON.` → `A MAN IN A PIT.`

segments.voice: The pit, then. Armenian tradition tells of Gregory, a Christian who served at the royal court and refused to worship the old gods. The king had him tortured and thrown into a pit, where, the story goes, he survived for years, fed in secret by a kind woman. Then the king fell gravely ill, and no one could heal him. Gregory was brought up out of the pit, prayed over the king, and the king was healed and baptized. Armenians call him Saint Gregory the Illuminator, the one who brought light. Next, the claim in today's line. Armenians say that when their king was baptized, the kingdom became Christian with him, and so they speak of Armenia as the first nation to adopt Christianity. It's a claim at the heart of how Armenians see themselves; historians discuss the details, and others make claims of their own. Then the alphabet. Tradition says a monk named Mesrop created the Armenian letters so the Bible could be read in Armenian, and the script is still in use today. A people with their own scripture in their own letters. Last, the Armenian Catholics. The ancient church of the Armenian people is the Armenian Apostolic Church. Some Armenian communities came into communion with Rome and became the Armenian Catholic Church, praying the same Armenian liturgy, with the same saints, the same music, the same letters. Armenians have known great suffering, and their churches, Apostolic and Catholic, have gone into exile together and prayed for the same dead.
screen: `GREGORY IN THE PIT.` · `THE KING HEALED AND BAPTIZED.` · `ARMENIANS SAY: THE FIRST NATION.` · `THEIR OWN LETTERS, THEIR OWN LITURGY.` · then, large: `UPON THE MOUNTAINS OF ARMENIA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember Armenia. Settle, and breathe. Picture a stone church on a high plateau, a mountain white against the sky, an old woman lighting a thin candle in sand. Picture the families scattered far from those mountains who still teach their children the letters. If you pray, you can pray for Armenia and its people, near and far, in your own words. If you don't, simply honor them: a people who kept a faith, a liturgy and an alphabet through a great deal. The bell holds the time.

The Armenian Catholics. Armenians in communion with Rome who pray the ancient Armenian liturgy and honor Saint Gregory the Illuminator, heirs of what Armenians call the first Christian nation. Today's word.
Your line: the first nation. Today, think of someone whose story starts in a pit, and treat them as someone who might yet bring light. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Armenian Catholics celebrate the Armenian Divine Liturgy in Classical Armenian, sharing its music, saints and feasts with the Armenian Apostolic Church, and honor Saint Gregory the Illuminator as the one who brought the faith to Armenia.

what a scholar hears: the claim of 'first Christian nation' rests on the tradition of King Tiridates's baptism by Gregory the Illuminator; historians discuss the dating, and the claim is central to Armenian identity.

sources.ref: Tradition of Saint Gregory the Illuminator

notes: 'First nation to adopt Christianity' is presented as what Armenians say, with 'historians discuss the details, and others make claims of their own'. No date given (traditionally 301). Confirm framing.

Gregory's pit (Khor Virap), survival 'for years' fed by a woman, and King Tiridates's healing and baptism follow the Agathangelos tradition; marked as tradition. Tradition says thirteen years; the number is omitted. Confirm.
The Armenian Apostolic Church is called 'the great church of the Armenian people'; no proportions given. Confirm.
'Armenians have known great suffering ... gone into exile together and prayed for the same dead' alludes to the Armenian Genocide without naming it, dates or numbers. Confirm tone.

Hook quote is Genesis 8:4 with an ellipsis: 'The ark rested … upon the mountains of Armenia'. Douay-Rheims (following the Vulgate) reads 'And the ark rested in the seventh month, the seven and twentieth day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia.' Sources quote only the final phrase. Confirm.
Ararat described as a mountain Armenians 'call Ararat' and look across at; it lies in present-day Turkey. Confirm wording.
Original: Հայաստան (Hayastan); confirm spelling and pronunciation.

Editor: hook no longer tells the listener how Armenians have 'long' felt about Ararat (now: tradition ties the mountain to the story); 'the great church' and 'date their nationhood from that day' softened; corrected the review note's Douay-Rheims wording of Genesis 8:4 (the Vulgate-based text has the twenty-seventh day); varied teach and practice openers.
